(ii) Bulky tertiary halide + strong base (KOH) favours E2 elimination over SN2, giving the alkene
(iii)&(iv)&(v) are straightforward SN2 substitution/Williamson-type reactions with the given nucleophile (OH⁻, CN⁻, phenoxide)
(vi) SOCl2 converts –OH to –Cl cleanly (byproducts SO2 and HCl gas escape, giving a pure product)
(vii)&(viii) HBr addition to an alkene follows Markovnikov's rule — H adds to the carbon with more H's already, Br to the more substituted carbon (via the more stable carbocation)

question:
Write the mechanism of the following reaction:
nBuBr + KCN → nBuCN
solution: This is an SN2 (bimolecular nucleophilic substitution) reaction. The cyanide ion (CN⁻, from KCN) acts as the nucleophile and attacks the electrophilic carbon of n-butyl bromide from the side directly opposite (backside) to the leaving bromide ion, in a single concerted step. As the C–CN bond begins to form, the C–Br bond simultaneously begins to break, passing through a trigonal bipyramidal transition state in which the carbon is partially bonded to both CN and Br; this backside attack causes inversion of configuration at the carbon (Walden inversion). The bromide ion (Br⁻) departs as the leaving group, giving n-butyl cyanide (pentanenitrile) and KBr.
steps: SN2 is a single-step, concerted mechanism: nucleophile attack and leaving group departure happen simultaneously
CN⁻ attacks the δ+ carbon of n-BuBr from the face opposite to Br (backside attack), forming a pentacoordinate (trigonal bipyramidal) transition state
As the new C–C(N) bond forms, the C–Br bond breaks and Br⁻ leaves, with inversion of configuration at the carbon centre (Walden inversion)
Product: n-BuCN (pentanenitrile) + Br⁻ (as KBr)

question:
Arrange the compounds of each set in order of reactivity towards SN2 displacement:
(i) 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane, 1-Bromopentane, 2-Bromopentane
(ii) 1-Bromo-3-methylbutane, 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane, 2-Bromo-3-methylbutane
(iii) 1-Bromobutane, 1-Bromo-2,2-dimethylpropane, 1-Bromo-2-methylbutane, 1-Bromo-3-methylbutane.

(i) 1-Bromopentane > 2-Bromopentane > 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane.
(ii) 1-Bromo-3-methylbutane > 2-Bromo-3-methylbutane > 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane.
(iii) 1-Bromobutane > 1-Bromo-3-methylbutane > 1-Bromo-2-methylbutane > 1-Bromo-2,2-dimethylpropane (neopentyl bromide).

question: Out of C6H5CH2Cl and C6H5CHClC6H5, which is more easily hydrolysed by aqueous KOH.
solution: C6H5CHClC6H5 (diphenylchloromethane / benzhydryl chloride) is hydrolysed more easily (faster) than C6H5CH2Cl (benzyl chloride).
steps: Both undergo hydrolysis primarily via an SN1 pathway (benzylic carbocation intermediate, stabilised by resonance with the adjacent aromatic ring)

C6H5CHClC6H5 ionises to a diphenylmethyl (benzhydryl) carbocation, which is stabilised by resonance delocalisation into TWO phenyl rings, making it considerably more stable than the benzyl cation (stabilised by only ONE phenyl ring) formed from C6H5CH2Cl
Greater carbocation stability means a faster SN1 reaction, so the diphenyl compound hydrolyses faster

question: p-Dichlorobenzene has higher m.p. than those of o- and m-isomers. Discuss.
solution: The melting point of a solid crystalline compound depends significantly on how symmetrically the molecules can pack in the crystal lattice — more symmetric molecules pack more closely and efficiently, giving stronger overall lattice (van der Waals/dispersion) forces and hence a higher melting point. The para-isomer of dichlorobenzene is highly symmetrical (the two Cl atoms are directly opposite each other on the ring), allowing it to pack very efficiently and closely in the solid lattice, giving it the highest melting point of the three isomers. The ortho- and especially the meta-isomers are less symmetrical, pack less efficiently in the crystal lattice, and consequently have lower melting points, even though all three isomers have essentially the same molecular formula, similar polarity and similar intermolecular forces in the liquid/gas state.
steps: Melting point depends heavily on crystal packing efficiency (symmetry), not just on intermolecular force strength per se
p-Dichlorobenzene has high molecular symmetry (Cl's at para/1,4 positions), allowing very close, efficient packing in the solid lattice
o- and m-isomers are less symmetric, pack less efficiently, giving weaker net lattice forces and hence lower melting points

(xi) Ethyl chloride → KCN → propanenitrile → H3O+ (acid hydrolysis) → propanoic acid.

(xviii) Benzene → Br2/FeBr3 → bromobenzene → Na, dry ether (Fittig/Wurtz-Fittig) → diphenyl (biphenyl).
(xix) tert-Butyl bromide → alc. KOH (elimination) → 2-methylpropene → HBr, peroxide (anti-Markovnikov addition) → isobutyl bromide (1-bromo-2-methylpropane).
(xx) Aniline → CHCl3 + alc. KOH (carbylamine reaction) → phenyl isocyanide (C6H5NC).

KOH/NaOH substitution, Finkelstein (NaI/acetone) and Swarts (AgF) halide exchange, Wurtz/Wurtz–Fittig coupling, Sandmeyer reaction, diazotisation, haloform reaction, carbylamine reaction, and directed aromatic substitution (o,p- vs m-directors)

question: The treatment of alkyl chlorides with aqueous KOH leads to the formation of alcohols but in the presence of alcoholic KOH, alkenes are major products. Explain.
solution: Aqueous KOH provides hydroxide ion (OH⁻) which, being highly solvated and less basic but still a good nucleophile in the polar protic water solvent, preferentially attacks the electrophilic carbon of the alkyl halide as a nucleophile, favouring the substitution (SN1/SN2) pathway to give an alcohol. Alcoholic KOH (KOH dissolved in ethanol) provides a less hydrated, more accessible/more basic ethoxide-influenced hydroxide that behaves predominantly as a strong base rather than a nucleophile, preferentially abstracting a β-hydrogen from the alkyl halide, favouring the elimination (E1/E2) pathway to give the alkene as the major product.
steps: Nucleophilicity vs basicity of OH⁻ depends on the solvent environment
In water (aqueous KOH), OH⁻ is heavily solvated/hydrogen-bonded, reducing its basicity relative to its nucleophilicity, so it favours substitution (attack at carbon) → alcohol
In ethanol (alcoholic KOH), OH⁻ is less solvated and acts as a stronger base, favouring proton abstraction from a β-carbon (elimination) → alkene

question:
What happens when
(i) n-butyl chloride is treated with alcoholic KOH,
(ii) bromobenzene is treated with Mg in the presence of dry ether,
(iii) chlorobenzene is subjected to hydrolysis,
(iv) ethyl chloride is treated with aqueous KOH,
(v) methyl bromide is treated with sodium in the presence of dry ether,
(vi) methyl chloride is treated with KCN?
solution:
(i) E2 elimination occurs, giving but-1-ene (and possibly some but-2-ene as byproduct): CH3CH2CH2CH2Cl + alc. KOH → CH3CH2CH=CH2 + KCl + H2O.
(ii) Grignard reagent forms: C6H5Br + Mg (dry ether) → C6H5MgBr (phenylmagnesium bromide).
(iii) Chlorobenzene resists ordinary hydrolysis (due to partial double bond character of C–Cl from resonance with the ring, and the sp² carbon is less accessible to nucleophilic attack); it requires drastic/vigorous conditions — fusion with NaOH at high temperature (623 K) and high pressure (300 atm) — to hydrolyse to phenol: C6H5Cl + 2NaOH (623K, 300 atm) → C6H5ONa + NaCl + H2O, followed by acidification to give phenol.
(iv) SN2 substitution occurs (aqueous KOH favours substitution, primary halide, unhindered): CH3CH2Cl + aq. KOH → CH3CH2OH + KCl.
(v) Wurtz reaction occurs: 2CH3Br + 2Na (dry ether) → CH3–CH3 (ethane) + 2NaBr.
(vi) SN2 substitution occurs (C-attack of the ambident CN⁻ nucleophile, methyl halide unhindered): CH3Cl + KCN → CH3CN (acetonitrile/methyl cyanide) + KCl.
steps: (i) Primary halide + alcoholic (strongly basic) KOH → E2 elimination → alkene
(ii) Aryl halide + Mg/dry ether → aryl Grignard reagent (C6H5MgBr)

(iii) Aryl halides are far less reactive to nucleophilic substitution than alkyl halides (C–X has partial double bond character, sp² carbon), needing forcing conditions (high T, high P, NaOH) to hydrolyse to phenol
(iv) Primary halide + aqueous (nucleophilic) KOH → SN2 substitution → alcohol
(v) Alkyl halide + Na/dry ether → Wurtz coupling → symmetric alkane (here, ethane from two methyl groups)
(vi) Alkyl halide + KCN → SN2 substitution via carbon attack of the ambident CN⁻ → nitrile (alkyl cyanide)

(x) 4-Chloro-3-ethylbutan-1-ol (note: as commonly given, 4-chloro on a 4-carbon chain with a 3-ethyl substituent implies a 5-carbon numbering context; structure follows the name literally).
solution:
(i) (CH3)2C(OH)CH2CH3 — tertiary alcohol.
(ii) C6H5CH2CH(OH)CH3.
(iii) HOCH2CH2C(CH3)(OH)CH2C(CH3)2OH (triol with OH at C1, C3, C5 of a hexane chain bearing methyls at C3 and C5).
(iv) Benzene ring with OH at C1 and ethyl groups at C2 and C3.

question:
(i) Draw the structures of all isomeric alcohols of molecular formula C5H12O and give their IUPAC names.
(ii) Classify the isomers of alcohols in question 7.3 (i) as primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols.
solution:
The 8 isomeric alcohols of C5H12O are:
(a) CH3CH2CH2CH2CH2OH, Pentan-1-ol — primary
(b) CH3CH2CH2CH(OH)CH3, Pentan-2-ol — secondary
(c) CH3CH2CH(OH)CH2CH3, Pentan-3-ol — secondary
(d) (CH3)2CHCH2CH2OH, 3-Methylbutan-1-ol — primary
(e) (CH3)2CHCH(OH)CH3, 3-Methylbutan-2-ol — secondary
(f) CH3CH2C(CH3)2OH, 2-Methylbutan-2-ol — tertiary
(g) (CH3)3CCH2OH, 2,2-Dimethylpropan-1-ol (neopentyl alcohol) — primary
(h) CH3CH2CH(CH3)CH2OH, 2-Methylbutan-1-ol — primary.
steps: Systematically enumerate all distinct C5H12O carbon skeletons (straight chain pentanol, methylbutanols, dimethylpropanol) with –OH at every non-equivalent carbon position
For each structure, determine whether the carbon bearing –OH is attached to 1, 2, or 3 other carbons, classifying it as primary, secondary or tertiary respectively
This gives 8 isomers total: 4 primary (a,d,g,h), 3 secondary (b,c,e), 1 tertiary (f)

question: Explain why propanol has higher boiling point than that of the hydrocarbon, butane?
solution: Propan-1-ol (b.p. ≈ 97°C) and butane (b.p. ≈ 0°C) have comparable molecular masses, but propanol's molecules contain an –OH group that allows extensive intermolecular hydrogen bonding between propanol molecules. Butane, being a non-polar hydrocarbon, can only engage in weak van der Waals (London dispersion) forces. Since hydrogen bonds are considerably stronger than van der Waals forces, significantly more thermal energy is required to overcome the hydrogen-bonded network and vaporise propanol, giving it a much higher boiling point than butane despite their similar molar masses.
steps: Compare intermolecular forces, not just molecular mass: propanol has an –OH group capable of hydrogen bonding; butane, a non-polar hydrocarbon, has only weak dispersion forces
Hydrogen bonds are much stronger than dispersion forces, requiring more energy to break during vaporisation
Hence propanol boils at a much higher temperature than butane of comparable molecular weight

question: Alcohols are comparatively more soluble in water than hydrocarbons of comparable molecular masses. Explain this fact.
solution: Alcohols contain a polar –OH group that can form hydrogen bonds with water molecules (both as a hydrogen-bond donor via its O–H and as an acceptor via the lone pairs on O), allowing alcohol molecules to be readily incorporated into water's hydrogen-bonded network, hence they dissolve appreciably in water (especially lower alcohols, fully miscible). Hydrocarbons are non-polar and cannot form hydrogen bonds with water; mixing a hydrocarbon with water would require breaking water's strong hydrogen-bonded structure without any compensating favourable interaction with the hydrocarbon, which is energetically unfavourable, so hydrocarbons of comparable molecular mass are essentially insoluble in water.
steps: Solubility in water depends on the ability to hydrogen bond with water, not just on molecular size/mass
Alcohols' –OH group can donate and accept hydrogen bonds with water, favouring mixing
Non-polar hydrocarbons cannot hydrogen bond with water, so replacing water-water H-bonds with hydrocarbon-water contacts is unfavourable, giving low solubility

question: What is meant by hydroboration-oxidation reaction? Illustrate it with an example.
solution: Hydroboration-oxidation is a two-step method for converting an alkene into an alcohol with anti-Markovnikov regiochemistry and syn (same-face) stereochemistry, without any carbocation rearrangement. In the first step (hydroboration), diborane (B2H6, or an equivalent borane reagent) adds across the C=C double bond, with boron attaching to the less substituted (less hindered) carbon and hydrogen to the more substituted carbon, forming a trialkylborane. In the second step (oxidation), the trialkylborane is treated with hydrogen peroxide in the presence of aqueous NaOH, which replaces the C–B bond with a C–OH bond (with retention of configuration), giving the anti-Markovnikov alcohol. Example: CH3CH=CH2 (propene) + B2H6 → (CH3CH2CH2)3B → [H2O2/NaOH] → 3 CH3CH2CH2OH (propan-1-ol, the anti-Markovnikov product, rather than propan-2-ol which would form via simple acid-catalysed hydration).
steps: Step 1 (hydroboration): B2H6 adds across C=C; B bonds to the less hindered/less substituted carbon, H to the more substituted carbon (anti-Markovnikov orientation)
Step 2 (oxidation): H2O2/NaOH replaces the C–B bond with C–OH, with retention of configuration at that carbon
Net result: overall anti-Markovnikov, syn addition of H and OH across the double bond, without carbocation rearrangement — e.g. propene → propan-1-ol

question: Give the structures and IUPAC names of monohydric phenols of molecular formula, C7H8O.
solution:
There are five isomers of C7H8O that are monohydric phenols (cresols) plus one that is not a phenol (anisole, a methyl ether, included here for completeness of the formula though it is not itself a phenol):
(1) 2-Methylphenol (o-cresol) — CH3 at position ortho to OH.
(2) 3-Methylphenol (m-cresol) — CH3 at position meta to OH.
(3) 4-Methylphenol (p-cresol) — CH3 at position para to OH.
(Note: methoxybenzene / anisole, C6H5OCH3, also has formula C7H8O but is an ether, not a phenol, so it is excluded from the phenol isomer count.)
steps: C7H8O with a benzene ring and a free phenolic –OH plus a methyl substituent gives the three cresol isomers (ortho, meta, para), based on the relative position of –CH3 to –OH on the ring
Anisole (C6H5OCH3) also matches formula C7H8O but is an ether (the O is not directly bonded as –OH to the ring), so it is not counted among the 'monohydric phenols' asked for

question: While separating a mixture of ortho and para nitrophenols by steam distillation, name the isomer which will be steam volatile. Give reason.
solution: ortho-Nitrophenol is steam volatile. This is because in the ortho isomer, the –OH and –NO2 groups are close enough to form an intramolecular hydrogen bond (chelation), which prevents/reduces intermolecular hydrogen bonding (association) between molecules, keeping individual molecules relatively free and giving the compound a lower boiling point and higher volatility, making it steam-distillable. In the para isomer, intramolecular H-bonding is geometrically impossible (the groups are too far apart), so p-nitrophenol molecules engage extensively in intermolecular hydrogen bonding (association), giving it a much higher boiling point/lower volatility, so it is not steam volatile (remains in the distillation flask).
steps: Steam volatility correlates with lower boiling point / weaker intermolecular association
o-Nitrophenol forms an intramolecular H-bond (5- or 6-membered ring chelate) between adjacent -OH and -NO2, which blocks intermolecular H-bonding between different molecules

p-Nitrophenol cannot form an intramolecular H-bond (groups too far apart) and instead engages in strong intermolecular H-bonding/association, raising its boiling point and making it non-volatile in steam

question: Give the equations of reactions for the preparation of phenol from cumene.
solution: Cumene (isopropylbenzene) is first air-oxidised (in the presence of a small amount of catalyst) to cumene hydroperoxide: C6H5CH(CH3)2 + O2 → C6H5C(CH3)2OOH. The cumene hydroperoxide is then treated with dilute acid (H3O+), which causes rearrangement and cleavage to give phenol and acetone: C6H5C(CH3)2OOH + H3O+ → C6H5OH + (CH3)2C=O + H2O.
steps: Step 1: Air oxidation of cumene (autoxidation) gives cumene hydroperoxide via a free-radical chain mechanism
Step 2: Acid-catalysed hydrolysis/rearrangement of the hydroperoxide gives phenol and acetone as co-products (this is the industrial 'cumene process' for manufacturing phenol)

question: Write chemical reaction for the preparation of phenol from chlorobenzene.
solution: Chlorobenzene is heated with aqueous NaOH under drastic conditions (623 K and 300 atm pressure) via nucleophilic aromatic substitution (Dow process): C6H5Cl + 2NaOH → (623K, 300 atm) → C6H5ONa + NaCl + H2O. The resulting sodium phenoxide is then acidified (with dilute HCl) to give free phenol: C6H5ONa + HCl → C6H5OH + NaCl.
steps: Chlorobenzene's C–Cl bond has partial double-bond character (resonance with the ring), making it resistant to nucleophilic substitution under mild conditions, so forcing conditions (very high temperature and pressure) are needed
Reaction with NaOH gives sodium phenoxide, which is then acidified to liberate phenol — this is the industrial Dow process

question: Write the mechanism of hydration of ethene to yield ethanol.
solution: Acid-catalysed hydration of ethene proceeds by an electrophilic addition (Markovnikov) mechanism via a carbocation intermediate. Step 1: A proton (H⁺, from dilute H2SO4/H3O⁺) is added electrophilically to the π-bond of ethene, forming a primary carbocation, CH3CH2⁺ (and regenerating HSO4⁻/being released from H3O⁺ to water). Step 2: Water (a nucleophile) attacks the electrophilic carbocation, forming a protonated alcohol (oxonium ion), CH3CH2OH2⁺. Step 3: Loss of a proton from the oxonium ion (deprotonation, e.g. by another water molecule acting as base) gives the neutral product, ethanol, CH3CH2OH, regenerating the H⁺ catalyst.
steps: Step 1: Electrophilic addition of H⁺ to the alkene π-bond generates a carbocation (Markovnikov-type addition)
Step 2: Nucleophilic attack of water's oxygen lone pair on the carbocation forms a protonated alcohol (oxonium ion)
Step 3: Deprotonation of the oxonium ion by another water molecule gives the neutral alcohol product and regenerates the H⁺ catalyst

question: You are given benzene, conc. H2SO4 and NaOH. Write the equations for the preparation of phenol using these reagents.
solution: Step 1: Benzene is sulphonated with conc. H2SO4 (fuming, or with SO3) to give benzenesulphonic acid: C6H6 + H2SO4 → C6H5SO3H + H2O. Step 2: The benzenesulphonic acid is fused with NaOH (solid, at high temperature) to convert the –SO3H group to –ONa via nucleophilic displacement: C6H5SO3H + 2NaOH → C6H5ONa + Na2SO3 + H2O. Step 3: Acidification of sodium phenoxide (e.g. with dilute HCl or excess H2SO4) gives free phenol: C6H5ONa + HCl → C6H5OH + NaCl.
steps: Step 1: Sulphonate benzene with conc. H2SO4 to introduce –SO3H
Step 2: Alkali fusion (NaOH, high temperature) converts –SO3H to –ONa (sodium phenoxide)
Step 3: Acidify sodium phenoxide to liberate phenol

question:
Show how will you synthesise:
(i) 1-phenylethanol from a suitable alkene.
(ii) cyclohexylmethanol using an alkyl halide by an SN2 reaction.
(iii) pentan-1-ol using a suitable alkyl halide?
solution:
(i) Styrene (phenylethene, C6H5CH=CH2) is treated with B2H6 followed by H2O2/NaOH (hydroboration-oxidation, anti-Markovnikov) to give 1-phenylethanol, C6H5CH(OH)CH3 — wait, anti-Markovnikov would place OH on the terminal carbon giving 2-phenylethanol; to obtain the benzylic alcohol 1-phenylethanol (OH on the carbon attached to the ring), simple Markovnikov acid-catalysed hydration (dilute H2SO4/H2O) of styrene is used instead, since the more stable benzylic carbocation forms preferentially: C6H5CH=CH2 + H2O (H+) → C6H5CH(OH)CH3.
(ii) Bromomethylcyclohexane (cyclohexylmethyl bromide, C6H11CH2Br) is treated with aqueous NaOH/KOH via SN2 substitution: C6H11CH2Br + NaOH → C6H11CH2OH (cyclohexylmethanol) + NaBr.
(iii) 1-Bromopentane (n-pentyl bromide) is treated with aqueous KOH via SN2 substitution: CH3CH2CH2CH2CH2Br + KOH(aq) → CH3CH2CH2CH2CH2OH (pentan-1-ol) + KBr.
steps: (i) Markovnikov (acid-catalysed) hydration of styrene favours formation of the more stable benzylic carbocation, placing OH directly on the ring-attached carbon to give 1-phenylethanol
(ii) A primary alkyl halide bearing the target carbon skeleton (cyclohexylmethyl bromide) undergoes straightforward SN2 hydrolysis with aqueous hydroxide to give the primary alcohol
(iii) Similarly, 1-bromopentane undergoes SN2 hydrolysis with aqueous KOH to directly give pentan-1-ol

question: Give two reactions that show the acidic nature of phenol. Compare acidity of phenol with that of ethanol.
solution: (1) Phenol reacts with aqueous NaOH to form sodium phenoxide and water (an acid-base neutralisation, showing phenol is acidic enough to react with a base): C6H5OH + NaOH → C6H5ONa + H2O. (2) Phenol reacts with active metals like sodium to liberate hydrogen gas (like other weak acids/alcohols reacting with reactive metals): 2C6H5OH + 2Na → 2C6H5ONa + H2. Comparison: Phenol (pKa ≈ 10) is considerably more acidic than ethanol (pKa ≈ 16), because the phenoxide ion (conjugate base of phenol) is stabilised by resonance delocalisation of the negative charge into the aromatic ring, whereas the ethoxide ion (conjugate base of ethanol) has no such resonance stabilisation and is destabilised further by the electron-donating (+I) effect of the alkyl group. Unlike ethanol, phenol reacts with aqueous NaOH itself (ethanol does not, since ethanol is too weak an acid to be deprotonated by hydroxide).
steps: Reaction with NaOH (phenol reacts to form phenoxide; ethanol does not react appreciably with NaOH) demonstrates phenol's greater acidity directly
Reaction with reactive metal (Na) liberating H2 gas is a general test for an acidic O–H, shown by both, but phenol reacts faster/more vigorously

Phenoxide ion is resonance-stabilised (negative charge delocalised over the ring), while ethoxide has no such stabilisation and is destabilised by the +I effect of the ethyl group — hence phenol (pKa≈10) is a much stronger acid than ethanol (pKa≈16)

question: Explain why is ortho nitrophenol more acidic than ortho methoxyphenol?
solution: The nitro group (–NO2) is strongly electron-withdrawing (both by induction and resonance), which stabilises the phenoxide ion formed after deprotonation by further delocalising/dispersing the negative charge (through resonance onto the nitro oxygens as well as the ring), making ortho-nitrophenol more acidic. The methoxy group (–OCH3), in contrast, is electron-donating by resonance (its lone pair donates into the ring), which would destabilise the negative charge of the phenoxide ion (intensify electron density where it's not wanted) and also has a comparatively small electron-withdrawing inductive effect that only partly compensates; the net effect is that methoxy makes the phenol less acidic than unsubstituted phenol at ortho position, and much less acidic than nitro-substituted phenol.
steps: Compare the electronic effect of each substituent on the stability of the resulting phenoxide (conjugate base) ion
–NO2 (strong −I and −M, electron-withdrawing) stabilises the negative charge of the phenoxide via resonance and induction, increasing acidity
–OCH3 (net electron-donating by resonance, +M dominates over −I) destabilises the phenoxide's negative charge, decreasing acidity relative to nitrophenol

question: Explain how does the –OH group attached to a carbon of benzene ring activate it towards electrophilic substitution?
solution: In phenol, one of the lone pairs of electrons on the oxygen atom of the –OH group is delocalised into the aromatic ring through resonance (conjugation with the π-system), which increases the electron density at the ortho and para positions of the ring (shown by additional resonance structures placing negative charge at o- and p-carbons). This heightened electron density makes the ring much more nucleophilic/reactive towards electrophiles compared to benzene itself, so the –OH group activates the ring towards electrophilic substitution reactions (and directs incoming electrophiles predominantly to the ortho and para positions).
steps: The oxygen lone pair of –OH is conjugated (delocalised) into the aromatic π-system via resonance
This resonance donation increases electron density specifically at the ortho and para ring positions
Higher electron density makes the ring a better nucleophile, so it reacts faster with electrophiles (activation) and preferentially at o/p positions (orientation)

question:
Give equations of the following reactions:
(i) Oxidation of propan-1-ol with alkaline KMnO4 solution.
(ii) Bromine in CS2 with phenol.
(iii) Dilute HNO3 with phenol.
(iv) Treating phenol wih chloroform in presence of aqueous NaOH.
solution:
(i) CH3CH2CH2OH + [O] (alkaline KMnO4) → CH3CH2COOH (propanoic acid) — oxidation proceeds all the way to the carboxylic acid via the aldehyde under these vigorous conditions.
(ii) C6H5OH + Br2 (in CS2, a non-polar solvent, low temperature) → predominantly monobromination, giving mainly p-bromophenol (with some o-bromophenol) — the use of a non-polar solvent at low temperature moderates the otherwise very fast reaction and avoids polysubstitution.
(iii) C6H5OH + dilute HNO3 (room temperature) → a mixture of o-nitrophenol and p-nitrophenol (o,p-nitration; o-isomer can be separated by steam distillation, being steam volatile as in Q7.8).
(iv) C6H5OH + CHCl3 + aq. NaOH (Reimer-Tiemann reaction, warm) → salicylaldehyde (2-hydroxybenzaldehyde) after acidification: gives o-hydroxybenzaldehyde as the major product, via a dichlorocarbene intermediate.
steps: (i) Primary alcohols are oxidised by strong oxidants like alkaline KMnO4 all the way to carboxylic acids (via the aldehyde intermediate, which is further oxidised under these conditions)
(ii) A non-polar solvent (CS2) and low temperature moderate the very reactive phenol ring, allowing controlled monobromination (mainly para, plus some ortho)
(iii) Dilute nitric acid nitrates phenol at both o- and p- positions (o,p-directing effect of OH), giving a separable mixture
(iv) Reimer-Tiemann reaction: phenol + CHCl3/NaOH generates a dichlorocarbene electrophile that substitutes mainly ortho to OH, giving (after hydrolysis) salicylaldehyde

question:
Explain the following with an example.
(i) Kolbe's reaction.
(ii) Reimer-Tiemann reaction.
(iii) Williamson ether synthesis.
(iv) Unsymmetrical ether.
solution:
(i) Kolbe's reaction: Sodium phenoxide is treated with CO2 under pressure and heated, followed by acidification, to introduce a –COOH group predominantly at the ortho position via electrophilic aromatic substitution by CO2 (the phenoxide oxygen directs the incoming electrophile), giving salicylic acid: C6H5ONa + CO2 → (heat, pressure) → sodium salicylate → (H3O+) → 2-hydroxybenzoic acid (salicylic acid).
(ii) Reimer-Tiemann reaction: Phenol is treated with chloroform and aqueous NaOH; NaOH generates a dichlorocarbene (:CCl2) from CHCl3, which attacks the phenoxide ring (mainly ortho position) to eventually give, after hydrolysis, an aromatic aldehyde: C6H5OH + CHCl3 + NaOH → (warm, then H3O+) → salicylaldehyde (2-hydroxybenzaldehyde).
(iii) Williamson ether synthesis: An alkyl halide is treated with sodium alkoxide (or sodium phenoxide) in an SN2 reaction to form an ether: R–X + R'ONa → R–O–R' + NaX. Example: CH3Br + C2H5ONa → CH3–O–C2H5 (methoxyethane) + NaBr.
(iv) Unsymmetrical (mixed) ether: an ether in which the two alkyl/aryl groups attached to the oxygen atom are different from each other, e.g. methoxyethane (CH3–O–C2H5), as opposed to a symmetrical ether like diethyl ether (C2H5–O–C2H5) where both groups are the same.
steps: (i) Kolbe's reaction: electrophilic carboxylation of phenoxide with CO2 gives salicylic acid
(ii) Reimer-Tiemann: dichlorocarbene generated from CHCl3+NaOH substitutes onto the phenol ring (ortho), giving an aromatic aldehyde after hydrolysis
(iii) Williamson synthesis: SN2 reaction between an alkyl halide and a metal alkoxide/phenoxide gives an ether
(iv) Unsymmetrical ether: the two R groups on either side of the ether oxygen are different

question: Write the mechanism of acid dehydration of ethanol to yield ethene.
solution: Acid-catalysed dehydration of ethanol to ethene proceeds via an E1 mechanism: Step 1 (protonation): the oxygen of ethanol is protonated by H2SO4, converting the poor leaving group –OH into a good leaving group, –OH2⁺ (protonated alcohol/oxonium ion): CH3CH2OH + H⁺ → CH3CH2OH2⁺. Step 2 (loss of water, rate-determining): the C–O bond breaks heterolytically, water leaves as a neutral molecule, generating a carbocation, CH3CH2⁺: CH3CH2OH2⁺ → CH3CH2⁺ + H2O. Step 3 (deprotonation/elimination): a base (HSO4⁻ or another ethanol molecule) removes a β-hydrogen from the carbocation, and the electrons form the new π-bond, giving ethene: CH3CH2⁺ → CH2=CH2 + H⁺ (regenerating the acid catalyst).
steps: Step 1: protonation of –OH by the acid catalyst converts it into a good leaving group (–OH2⁺)
Step 2 (rate-determining): loss of water generates a carbocation
Step 3: base removes a β-hydrogen, forming the alkene π-bond and regenerating the H⁺ catalyst (E1 mechanism)

question:
How are the following conversions carried out?
(i) Propene → Propan-2-ol.
(ii) Benzyl chloride → Benzyl alcohol.
(iii) Ethyl magnesium chloride → Propan-1-ol.
(iv) Methyl magnesium bromide → 2-Methylpropan-2-ol.
solution:
(i) Propene undergoes acid-catalysed Markovnikov hydration: CH3CH=CH2 + H2O (dil. H2SO4) → CH3CH(OH)CH3 (propan-2-ol).
(ii) Benzyl chloride is hydrolysed with aqueous NaOH (SN2/SN1): C6H5CH2Cl + NaOH(aq) → C6H5CH2OH (benzyl alcohol) + NaCl.
(iii) Ethylmagnesium chloride is reacted with formaldehyde (methanal) followed by acidic hydrolysis: C2H5MgCl + HCHO → C2H5CH2OMgCl → (H3O+) → C2H5CH2OH (propan-1-ol).
(iv) Methylmagnesium bromide is reacted with acetone (propanone) followed by acidic hydrolysis: CH3MgBr + (CH3)2CO → (CH3)3COMgBr → (H3O+) → (CH3)3COH (2-methylpropan-2-ol, tert-butanol).
steps: (i) Direct Markovnikov acid-catalysed hydration of the alkene gives the secondary alcohol
(ii) Simple aqueous alkaline hydrolysis converts the benzylic halide to the alcohol

(iii)&(iv) Grignard reagents react with carbonyl compounds (aldehydes/ketones) to form (after acidic workup) alcohols; a Grignard + formaldehyde gives a primary alcohol with one more carbon; a Grignard + ketone gives a tertiary alcohol

question:
Name the reagents used in the following reactions:
(i) Oxidation of a primary alcohol to carboxylic acid.
(ii) Oxidation of a primary alcohol to aldehyde.
(iii) Bromination of phenol to 2,4,6-tribromophenol.
(iv) Benzyl alcohol to benzoic acid.
(v) Dehydration of propan-2-ol to propene.
(vi) Butan-2-one to butan-2-ol.
solution:
(i) Acidified potassium permanganate (KMnO4/H⁺) or acidified potassium dichromate (K2Cr2O7/H2SO4) — strong oxidants that oxidise the primary alcohol fully to the carboxylic acid.
(ii) Pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC), or collidine + CrO3 (Collins reagent) — mild oxidants that stop oxidation at the aldehyde stage (since they cannot further oxidise the aldehyde in the absence of water).
(iii) Bromine water (excess Br2 in water, no catalyst needed since phenol is highly activated) — gives immediate white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol.
(iv) Acidified/alkaline KMnO4 (or acidified K2Cr2O7) — vigorous oxidant that converts the benzylic –CH2OH directly to –COOH.
(v) Concentrated H2SO4 (or conc. H3PO4/Al2O3, heated) — acid-catalysed dehydration.
(vi) Sodium borohydride, NaBH4 (or LiAlH4) — mild reducing agent that reduces the ketone carbonyl to a secondary alcohol.
steps: Match each named transformation to the standard reagent taught for it in the NCERT text: strong oxidants (KMnO4/K2Cr2O7 with H+) for alcohol→acid; mild selective oxidants (PCC) for alcohol→aldehyde without over-oxidation; Br2 water for the highly activated phenol ring's electrophilic tribromination; dehydrating acids (conc. H2SO4) for alcohol→alkene; hydride reducing agents (NaBH4/LiAlH4) for ketone→alcohol

question: Give reason for the higher boiling point of ethanol in comparison to methoxymethane.
solution: Ethanol (CH3CH2OH) and methoxymethane (dimethyl ether, CH3OCH3) are functional isomers (same molecular formula C2H6O), but ethanol has an –OH group with a hydrogen directly bonded to the electronegative oxygen, allowing extensive intermolecular hydrogen bonding between ethanol molecules. Methoxymethane has no O–H bond (the oxygen is bonded to two carbon atoms), so it cannot engage in hydrogen bonding between its own molecules, and only weaker dipole-dipole and van der Waals forces operate. Since hydrogen bonds are considerably stronger than these forces, significantly more energy is needed to vaporise ethanol, giving it a much higher boiling point (78°C) than methoxymethane (−24°C).
steps: Ethanol and methoxymethane are isomers (C2H6O) but differ in intermolecular forces due to functional group difference
Ethanol's O–H allows intermolecular hydrogen bonding; methoxymethane's ether oxygen has no attached H, so no such H-bonding is possible between its molecules
Hydrogen bonding is much stronger than the dipole-dipole/dispersion forces available to the ether, so ethanol has a far higher boiling point

question:
Write the names of reagents and equations for the preparation of the following ethers by Williamson's synthesis:
(i) 1-Propoxypropane
(ii) Ethoxybenzene
(iii) 2-Methoxy-2-methylpropane
(iv) 1-Methoxyethane
solution:
(i) Sodium propoxide + 1-bromopropane: CH3CH2CH2ONa + CH3CH2CH2Br → CH3CH2CH2–O–CH2CH2CH3 + NaBr.
(ii) Sodium phenoxide + bromoethane (or ethyl halide with the alkyl halide as the electrophile, since aryl halides cannot be used as the electrophilic partner in Williamson synthesis): C6H5ONa + C2H5Br → C6H5–O–C2H5 + NaBr.
(iii) Sodium methoxide + tert-butyl bromide is NOT favourable (tertiary halide gives elimination with the basic alkoxide); instead the correct combination uses the bulkier group as the alkoxide and methyl halide as the electrophile: (CH3)3CONa (sodium tert-butoxide) + CH3I → (CH3)3C–O–CH3 + NaI.
(iv) Sodium methoxide + bromoethane: CH3ONa + C2H5Br → CH3–O–C2H5 + NaBr.
steps: Williamson synthesis: R–X (alkyl halide, must be primary/methyl to favour SN2 over elimination) + R'–ONa (sodium alkoxide/phenoxide) → R–O–R' + NaX
For each target ether, split it at the C–O bond in the way that gives a good (primary/methyl, unhindered) alkyl halide component and an alkoxide/phenoxide component

For (iii), since the target has a bulky tert-butyl group on one side, that bulky group must be supplied as the ALKOXIDE (not the halide, which would favour elimination if tertiary) reacting with methyl iodide as the unhindered electrophile

question: Illustrate with examples the limitations of Williamson synthesis for the preparation of certain types of ethers.
solution: The Williamson synthesis proceeds by an SN2 mechanism, so it works best when the alkyl halide component is primary (unhindered). Its key limitations: (1) If a secondary or (especially) tertiary alkyl halide is used as the electrophilic component together with an alkoxide (a strong base), the strongly basic alkoxide tends to promote E2 elimination instead of substitution, giving an alkene as the major product rather than the desired ether — e.g. attempting to make tert-butyl methyl ether from sodium methoxide and tert-butyl bromide mostly gives 2-methylpropene instead. This is overcome by reversing the roles: using the bulky group as the alkoxide and methyl/primary halide as the electrophile (as in Q7.24(iii)). (2) Aryl (and vinyl) halides cannot be used as the electrophilic (halide) component at all, because the C–X bond in aryl/vinyl halides has partial double bond character and does not undergo SN2 substitution under these conditions (only alkyl halides work as the electrophile; the aryl group can only be introduced via a phenoxide as the nucleophile, e.g. anisole is made from sodium phenoxide + methyl iodide, not from chlorobenzene + sodium methoxide).
steps: The reaction requires an SN2-favourable alkyl halide; bulky (secondary/tertiary) halides undergo competing E2 elimination with the strongly basic alkoxide instead of substitution

Aryl and vinyl halides are unreactive as the electrophilic partner (their C–X bond does not undergo SN2), so an aryl group in the ether can only be introduced via the phenoxide/vinyloxide side, never via the halide side
These limitations mean the halide component must always be chosen as a primary alkyl halide, with the bulkier/aryl group supplied as the alkoxide/phenoxide nucleophile

question: How is 1-propoxypropane synthesised from propan-1-ol? Write mechanism of this reaction.
solution: 1-Propoxypropane (di-n-propyl ether) is prepared from propan-1-ol by acid-catalysed intermolecular dehydration: 2CH3CH2CH2OH → (conc. H2SO4, 413 K) → CH3CH2CH2–O–CH2CH2CH3 + H2O. Mechanism (SN2-type, via protonation then nucleophilic displacement of water): Step 1: one molecule of propan-1-ol is protonated by H2SO4 to form the oxonium ion, CH3CH2CH2OH2⁺. Step 2: a second molecule of propan-1-ol (acting as a nucleophile through its oxygen lone pair) attacks the electrophilic carbon of the protonated alcohol from the backside, displacing water (a good leaving group after protonation) in an SN2 fashion, forming a protonated ether: CH3CH2CH2OH2⁺ + CH3CH2CH2OH → CH3CH2CH2–O⁺H–CH2CH2CH3 + H2O. Step 3: loss of a proton from the protonated ether (deprotonation by another alcohol/water molecule) gives the neutral ether product, 1-propoxypropane, and regenerates the H⁺ catalyst.
steps: Overall: acid-catalysed intermolecular dehydration of two molecules of the same primary alcohol at 413 K gives the symmetrical ether
Mechanism step 1: protonation of one alcohol molecule's OH converts it to a good leaving group (–OH2⁺)
Step 2: SN2 attack of a second (nucleophilic) alcohol molecule's oxygen on this protonated species, displacing water and forming a protonated ether
Step 3: deprotonation of the protonated ether gives the neutral ether product and regenerates the acid catalyst

question: Preparation of ethers by acid dehydration of secondary or tertiary alcohols is not a suitable method. Give reason.
solution: Acid-catalysed dehydration of alcohols to form ethers proceeds via a carbocation-type (SN1-like) pathway when the alcohol is secondary or tertiary (since these alcohols readily form relatively stable secondary/tertiary carbocations under acidic conditions). Instead of being captured by a second alcohol molecule to form the ether (which is itself a comparatively slow/reversible process), such carbocations much more readily undergo elimination (E1) — losing a β-hydrogen to form the more thermodynamically stable alkene, since alkene formation is favoured over the intermolecular substitution needed for ether formation, especially at the higher temperatures typically used for dehydration. Hence with secondary/tertiary alcohols, dehydration predominantly gives alkenes rather than ethers, making this method unsuitable for those alcohols (it works well only for primary alcohols, where SN2 ether formation competes favourably against the less-easily-formed primary carbocation/E1 pathway).
steps: Secondary/tertiary alcohols readily form relatively stable carbocations under acid catalysis (SN1/E1-favourable conditions)
Such carbocations preferentially lose a β-H (E1 elimination) to give the more stable, thermodynamically favoured alkene, rather than being trapped by another alcohol molecule to form an ether

Hence acid dehydration of 2°/3° alcohols mainly yields alkenes, not ethers; only primary alcohols (which proceed via an SN2-like pathway, disfavouring elimination) give ethers efficiently by this method

question:
Write the equation of the reaction of hydrogen iodide with:
(i) 1-propoxypropane
(ii) methoxybenzene and
(iii) benzyl ethyl ether.
solution:
(i) CH3CH2CH2–O–CH2CH2CH3 + HI (excess, heat) → CH3CH2CH2OH + CH3CH2CH2I (initially), and with excess HI the alcohol is further converted: CH3CH2CH2OH + HI → CH3CH2CH2I + H2O, giving 2 mol of 1-iodopropane overall.
(ii) C6H5–O–CH3 + HI → C6H5OH (phenol) + CH3I. (The aryl–O bond is never cleaved because that would require nucleophilic attack at an sp² carbon, which does not occur; instead the weaker O–CH3 bond is cleaved by I⁻, with the alkyl group leaving as the alkyl iodide and the aryl group retained as phenol.)
(iii) C6H5CH2–O–C2H5 + HI → C6H5CH2I (benzyl iodide) + C2H5OH (preferentially; the benzylic C–O bond cleaves in preference to the ethyl C–O bond because the benzylic carbocation/SN1-type pathway is favoured, i.e. iodide attacks the benzylic carbon).
steps: Ethers are cleaved by excess concentrated HI via SN2 (for less hindered alkyl groups) or SN1 (for benzylic/allylic/tertiary groups), with I⁻ attacking the less hindered/more electrophilic carbon, releasing an alcohol which (with excess HI) is further converted to the corresponding alkyl iodide
For aryl alkyl ethers (methoxybenzene), the Ar–O bond is never broken (aryl carbon does not undergo nucleophilic substitution); only the alkyl–O bond cleaves, giving phenol + alkyl iodide
For benzyl ethers, the benzylic C–O bond cleaves preferentially (stabilised benzylic cation/transition state), giving benzyl iodide + the other alcohol

question: Explain the fact that in aryl alkyl ethers (i) the alkoxy group activates the benzene ring towards electrophilic substitution and (ii) it directs the incoming substituents to ortho and para positions in benzene ring.
solution: In an aryl alkyl ether (e.g. anisole, C6H5OCH3), one of the lone pairs on the ether oxygen is delocalised into the aromatic ring via resonance (conjugation), similar to phenol. (i) This electron donation increases the overall electron density of the ring compared to benzene, making the ring more reactive (a better nucleophile) towards electrophiles, i.e. it activates the ring towards electrophilic aromatic substitution. (ii) The resonance structures arising from this delocalisation place extra negative charge (electron density) specifically at the ortho and para carbons of the ring (not at the meta carbons), so an incoming electrophile preferentially attacks at these positions, making the alkoxy group an ortho, para-director.
steps: The ether oxygen's lone pair conjugates with the aromatic π-system by resonance (analogous to the –OH group in phenol)
(i) This resonance donation raises overall ring electron density, activating it towards electrophilic attack
(ii) The specific resonance structures place negative charge preferentially at ortho and para positions, directing electrophiles there

question: Write the mechanism of the reaction of HI with methoxymethane.
solution: Methoxymethane (dimethyl ether, CH3OCH3) reacts with HI by an SN2 mechanism (since both alkyl groups are methyl/primary, unhindered). Step 1: the ether oxygen is protonated by HI, converting it into a good leaving group as part of a protonated ether (oxonium ion): CH3OCH3 + HI → CH3O⁺(H)CH3 + I⁻. Step 2: the iodide ion (I⁻, a good nucleophile) attacks one of the electrophilic methyl carbons from the backside (SN2), displacing the neutral methanol as the leaving group and forming methyl iodide: CH3O⁺(H)CH3 + I⁻ → CH3I + CH3OH.
steps: Step 1: protonation of the ether oxygen by HI converts the poor leaving group (ether O) into a much better one (neutral alcohol as leaving group once displaced)
Step 2: I⁻ performs a backside SN2 attack on one of the methyl carbons (both are equally primary/unhindered here), cleaving that C–O bond and displacing methanol
Product: CH3I + CH3OH

question:
Write equations of the following reactions:
(i) Friedel-Crafts reaction – alkylation of anisole.
(ii) Nitration of anisole.
(iii) Bromination of anisole in ethanoic acid medium.
(iv) Friedel-Craft's acetylation of anisole.
solution:
(i) C6H5OCH3 + CH3Cl (AlCl3, anhydrous) → predominantly p-methylanisole (1-methoxy-4-methylbenzene, with some ortho isomer) + HCl.
(ii) C6H5OCH3 + conc. HNO3/conc. H2SO4 → predominantly p-nitroanisole (1-methoxy-4-nitrobenzene, with some ortho isomer).
(iii) C6H5OCH3 + Br2 (in CH3COOH, room temperature, no catalyst needed since ring is highly activated) → predominantly p-bromoanisole (1-bromo-4-methoxybenzene, plus minor ortho isomer).
(iv) C6H5OCH3 + CH3COCl (AlCl3, anhydrous) → predominantly p-methoxyacetophenone (1-(4-methoxyphenyl)ethan-1-one, plus minor ortho isomer) + HCl.
steps: Anisole's methoxy group is a strong activator and o,p-director (as in Q7.29), so in each electrophilic aromatic substitution the electrophile (alkyl cation, nitronium ion, Br⁺, acylium ion respectively) attacks predominantly at the para position (with some ortho product, minimised by steric hindrance from the OCH3 group)

(i) uses an alkyl halide + AlCl3 (Friedel-Crafts alkylation); (ii) uses the standard nitrating mixture; (iii) uses Br2 in acetic acid (no catalyst needed due to high ring reactivity); (iv) uses an acyl chloride + AlCl3 (Friedel-Crafts acylation)

question: When 3-methylbutan-2-ol is treated with HBr, the following reaction takes place (2-bromo-3-methylbutane rearranges to give 2-bromo-2-methylbutane as the major product). Give a mechanism for this reaction. (Hint: The secondary carbocation formed in step II rearranges to a more stable tertiary carbocation by a hydride ion shift from the 3rd carbon atom.)
solution: The reaction proceeds by an SN1 mechanism with carbocation rearrangement. Step 1 (protonation): the –OH of 3-methylbutan-2-ol, (CH3)2CHCH(OH)CH3, is protonated by HBr to give the oxonium ion, (CH3)2CHCH(OH2⁺)CH3. Step 2 (ionisation): loss of water generates a secondary carbocation at C2, (CH3)2CH–CH⁺–CH3. Step 3 (1,2-hydride shift / rearrangement): a hydrogen atom (as a hydride, H⁻) migrates from the adjacent C3 (which bears a methyl-substituted, more highly branched carbon) to the carbocation centre at C2, converting the less stable secondary carbocation into the more stable tertiary carbocation at C3: (CH3)2C⁺–CH2CH3 (i.e. the 2-methylbutan-2-yl cation). Step 4 (nucleophilic capture): the bromide ion (Br⁻, released in step 2) attacks this more stable tertiary carbocation, giving the rearranged major product, 2-bromo-2-methylbutane, (CH3)2C(Br)CH2CH3, rather than the unrearranged 2-bromo-3-methylbutane.
steps: Step 1: protonate –OH to create a good leaving group (–OH2⁺)
Step 2: ionisation (loss of water) generates a secondary carbocation at C2

Step 3: a 1,2-hydride shift from the adjacent (more substituted) C3 converts this secondary carbocation into the more stable tertiary carbocation, since SN1 reactions proceed via the most stable accessible carbocation
Step 4: Br⁻ captures the rearranged tertiary carbocation, giving the rearranged product (2-bromo-2-methylbutane) as the major product rather than the 'expected' unrearranged isomer
